title: HiMAP-Travel: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Planning for Long-Horizon Constrained Travel
one_liner: Split trip planning into one top-level budget keeper and several day planners so long plans stay within hard rules while the daily work runs in parallel.
lead: Planning a long trip is difficult for one long context window. As the plan grows day by day, the agent can forget the total budget, repeat places, or miss diversity rules. This paper addresses that failure by separating global resource allocation from local day planning, then adding a monitor that can reject local plans when they break shared constraints.

problem.h2: Why one long planning chain drifts off the rules
paras: A travel plan is not just a list of places. It must satisfy shared constraints across many days, such as a total budget cap, variety across locations, and limits on duplicate activities. A single sequential planner often loses track of those cross-day facts because each new day adds more context to carry forward.

That drift gets worse on long horizons because a locally good day can still break the whole trip. Spending too much on day two leaves too little for day six. Reusing the same attraction style may satisfy one day but fail the diversity goal for the trip. The paper asks how to keep global rules visible while still planning each day in detail.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Use a coordinator to allocate shared resources across days, let separate day executors plan in parallel, and put a transactional monitor in the middle so that invalid local plans are rejected before they damage the full itinerary.

panels.title: 1. A long trip has shared rules
panels.viz_args: Budget cap | no repeats | diverse activities
panels.caption: Every day must fit rules that apply to the full trip, not just to one local choice.

panels.title: 2. One sequential planner keeps carrying more context
panels.caption: As the context grows, the planner can miss earlier commitments.

panels.title: 3. Split the work by level
panels.viz_args: Coordinator sets limits; day planners fill each day
panels.caption: One part holds the global view while local planners focus on daily detail.

panels.title: 4. Check plans before accepting them
panels.viz_args: Monitor checks budget and duplicate constraints
panels.caption: A local plan can be rejected because it would violate a shared rule.

panels.title: 5. Parallel day planning speeds up the whole trip
panels.caption: The system keeps global constraints intact while several days are planned at once.

steps.text: A coordinator sets a budget and other high-level targets for each day because the trip-wide rules must be decided before local planning starts.
Day executors propose activities for their assigned day using the local budget and goals they received.
A monitor checks whether the proposed days still satisfy global constraints such as total cost and uniqueness because local plans can conflict with each other.

steps.b: Bargain when a day is infeasible
steps.text: If one day cannot satisfy its allocation, that executor rejects the sub-goal so the coordinator can re-plan with a different split.
All agents use one trained decision rule with different role conditioning so that the system learns common planning behavior while still acting differently by role.

paras: The paper changes travel planning from one long serial chain into a hierarchy. The top layer manages trip-wide resources and the lower layer fills in daily plans, with a monitor that can block invalid local outputs before they accumulate.
object.object: how planning authority is split across the trip

hidden.name: how much future room each current day decision leaves for the rest of the trip
paras: The key hidden quantity is future slack. A day planner sees only its local choices, but the real cost of those choices depends on how much budget, variety, and flexibility remain for later days. A meal or hotel that seems acceptable now may make the last days impossible.

HiMAP-Travel exposes that hidden quantity by forcing the coordinator to allocate resources up front and by letting the monitor reject proposals that would overuse shared slack. That helps because each day is planned against a visible budget and visible uniqueness rules, not against vague future hope.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the hidden trip-wide state that local day planners need help to respect.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how much freedom the trip still has after each local day plan is accepted.
The hierarchy makes global feasibility explicit through resource allocation and transactional constraint checks across parallel day agents.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: keep global constraints outside local day details
paras: A long serial planner fails because it mixes two jobs that should be separated. One job is global bookkeeping across the full trip. The other job is detailed day construction. When one agent does both jobs in one running chain, earlier budget and uniqueness facts are easy to lose.

The hierarchy works because the coordinator holds the trip-wide facts in a compact form, and day executors can focus on one local slice. The monitor is the second key piece because it prevents a local plan from being accepted only because it looks good on its own. Parallel day planning also cuts latency because several local plans are produced at the same time instead of one after another.

stages.s: Coordinator allocates money and goals across days
Day executors plan several days in parallel
A full itinerary that respects global rules and is produced faster because several day plans are built at the same time

math.h2: Choose day plans under a shared budget and shared rules
math.words: A simple summary is to maximize the total trip score across all days while forcing the sum of day costs to stay below the total budget and forcing duplicate-sensitive choices to remain within allowed limits.
math.equation: trip_score = sum(day_value_d) subject to sum(day_cost_d) <= total_budget and duplicate_count <= allowed_limit
symbols: total trip cost across all days
maximum allowed spend for the full trip
number of repeated items that violate uniqueness goals

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a three-day trip has a total budget of 300.
The coordinator allocates 90, 110, and 100 to the three days.
The day planners propose costs of 85, 120, and 96, so the total is 301.
The monitor rejects day two because 301 is above the full-trip budget and asks for a cheaper day-two plan.
A revised day-two plan costs 103, which brings the total to 284, so the trip becomes feasible.

math.note: The bargaining step matters because one day planner can say its current budget split is infeasible, which lets the coordinator repair the global allocation before the full itinerary is finalized.

charts.title: One long sequential planner
charts.note: A single chain drifts because the full set of trip-wide rules keeps growing as planning continues.

charts.title: HiMAP-Travel
charts.note: The paper reports stronger final-pass rates and lower delay because hierarchy preserves global rules while day work runs in parallel.

items.b: The coordinator can allocate resources poorly.
items.html: If the initial budget split is unrealistic, many day planners will reject their sub-goals because the assigned limits do not match what that day needs.
If the monitor forgets one global rule, a locally valid plan can still break the trip because accepted days are only as good as the checks that guard them.

items.b: Parallel days can still interact in hidden ways.
items.html: Two days may compete for the same scarce option or create awkward travel flow, which means the monitor may need richer cross-day checks than simple budget and duplicate counts.

The design works best when the coordinator carries only global facts, the day executors stay local, and the monitor enforces the full rule set because that separation keeps each part narrow and testable.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a trip planner with a fixed total budget, a no-repeat rule for attraction categories, and several days of planning. Compare one sequential planner against a HiMAP-style hierarchy with one coordinator, several day planners, and a monitor.

Track final pass rate on all hard rules, planning time, and the number of rejected day plans that required reallocation. The hierarchy should produce more valid trips because the monitor catches cross-day conflicts, and it should finish sooner because day planning happens in parallel.
demo.metric_eq: rule_pass_rate = valid_itineraries / total_itineraries ; speed_gain = sequential_time - hierarchical_time
demo.closing: The result should show that splitting global bookkeeping from local day construction is useful because the two jobs create different kinds of errors when they are forced into one long planning chain.
